entries.title: Pictish forces defeat Northumbria at Dun Nechtain
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Eastern Highlands and Angus regional reference, exact battlefield unknown
entries.summary: The encounter changed Northumbrian power in northern Britain and is independently attested from its precise location.
entries.detail: Dunnichen in Angus is the traditional candidate. Another historical and geographical analysis argues for Badenoch. The regional reference avoids choosing either place in the movie; the guide maps both hypotheses.
entries.uncertainty: The source establishes the battle and year. The pin is an editorial regional reference with no claim that fighting occurred there.

participants: Pictish forces led by Bridei son of Beli
warfare.outcome: Ecgfrith died and the Northumbrian force was defeated.

entries.title: The Wessex reeve is killed after a Northmen landing
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A chronicle describes ships arriving on the southern coast before the better-dated Lindisfarne raid.
entries.detail: The sources attach the encounter to the time of King Beorhtric. Later evidence is used to associate it with Portland and distinguish a recorded violent landing from later, large campaigns.
entries.uncertainty: The dating and localization are less firm than Lindisfarne’s. The origin port and path are unknown.

participants: Northmen recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
West Saxon reeve and local representatives
warfare.outcome: The visitors killed the official who approached them.

entries.title: Raiders burn Inis Pátraic off Skerries
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: St Patrick’s Island off Skerries, County Dublin
entries.summary: The account names an identifiable island and gives details of the attack’s effect on property and religious objects.
entries.detail: This follows an early annal about Rechru whose identification has been debated. Inis Pátraic is a firmer geographic anchor.
entries.uncertainty: The island is identifiable. The ships’ origin and movements between raids remain unknown.

participants: People in the island and surrounding district
warfare.outcome: The annal records burning, seizure of cattle tribute and the destruction of a shrine.

entries.title: Raiders burn the monastery on Iona
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The account is an early written record of an attack on this island monastery.
entries.detail: Later entries establish further attacks on the island. Different accounts of the monastery’s response also document shifting links between Iona and religious communities across the Irish Sea.
entries.uncertainty: The annals give the target and year; departure point and route are unknown.

warfare.outcome: The annals record burning at Iona.

entries.title: Norse raiders kill members of the community on Iona
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A separate entry from the earlier burning documents another major attack on Iona.
entries.detail: The reported toll comes from the annal. The violence contributed to a longer change in how the community operated across several sites.
entries.uncertainty: There is a known island target. The estimate and specific positions within the island come from sparse documentary evidence.

warfare.outcome: The annalist records the killing of dozens of people in the community.

entries.title: Norse force defeats the men of Fortriu
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Moray Firth area, Fortriu reference anchor only
entries.summary: An Irish annal reports a major military setback for the Pictish polity.
entries.detail: The record is important for political change in the ninth century. It provides no coordinates, exact attacker origin or account of what happened to the broader population.
entries.uncertainty: The map pin reflects a scholarly localization of Fortriu. Where the battle happened is unknown.

participants: Norse force named in the Annals of Ulster
Men of Fortriu and leaders including Eóganán son of Óengus
warfare.outcome: The annals record a defeat for Fortriu and the deaths of several named leaders.

entries.title: The Viking Great Army takes York
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The capture turned a major city into a center of the Viking army’s operations.
entries.detail: The army’s presence subsequently produced a different urban record of political administration and settlement. Capture and later city growth have separate dates.
entries.uncertainty: The sequence is documentary. The pin locates the city rather than an exact point of entry.

warfare.outcome: The army took York in 866; Northumbrian kings attempted to retake it the following year.

entries.title: Northumbrian rulers die in their attempt to retake York
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A Northumbrian counterattack followed the army’s capture of York the previous year.
entries.detail: The sequence shows that one place can be a campaign objective, a battle locality and later an urban center, with each claim relying on different evidence.
entries.uncertainty: The event is not mapped as continuous control over a larger territory.

participants: Northumbrian forces of Ælla and Osberht
warfare.outcome: The attack failed and both Northumbrian rulers were killed.

entries.title: Norse kings besiege Alt Clut at Dumbarton
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A four-month siege ended in the capture of the Brittonic stronghold, according to the Annals of Ulster.
entries.detail: This attack was against the power center at Alt Clut. Its effects should be read alongside the longer survival of a Brittonic polity around the Clyde.
entries.uncertainty: The pin locates the fortress. The annal gives no mapped siege lines.

participants: Amlaíb and Ímar and their forces
warfare.outcome: The attackers took and plundered the fortress after a prolonged siege.

entries.title: Harald’s forces prevail in the battle tradition associated with Hafrsfjord
entries.dateLabel: Late ninth century CE, conventional date 872
entries.dateMeaning: Broad period within which the historically uncertain battle is conventionally placed
entries.summary: Early poetry and later accounts associate a naval confrontation with Hafrsfjord.
entries.detail: Ongoing maritime archaeology studies the fjord. The battle is not a secure exact year for the creation of a state bounded like present-day Norway.
entries.uncertainty: 872 is a conventional date. The range represents a broad scholarly context and the pin identifies the fjord rather than a located battlefield.

participants: Harald Fairhair’s forces in the skaldic and saga tradition
Opposing regional forces in the same sources
warfare.outcome: The tradition records a victory for Harald; its precise historical effects are less clear.

entries.title: Amlaíb and Ímar return to Dublin with captives
entries.dateMeaning: Annal year of the return to Dublin
entries.place: Alt Clut campaign context, with Dublin return endpoint
entries.summary: After the siege of Alt Clut, an annal records the fleet’s return from Alba and the forcible transfer of captives.
entries.detail: Dublin and the Clyde stronghold give supported campaign and return endpoints. The chronicle’s ship total is a reported figure and individual embarkation places cannot be located.
entries.uncertainty: The line is schematic. The sources establish the fortress campaign and the arrival, not the precise course or all the places where people were seized.

participants: Amlaíb and Ímar and their forces
Captive Angles, Britons and Picts named by the annal
warfare.outcome: The fleet arrived at Dublin with people taken captive in the campaign.

entries.title: Cenél nEógain and Norse allies storm Dún Sobairche
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A recorded alliance between a local Irish group and Norse forces captured the coastal fortress.
entries.detail: The entry appears near the annal concerning the return of Amlaíb and Ímar to Dublin. It directly documents cooperation across political groups normally assigned different identities.
entries.uncertainty: The precise composition of the allied force and the parts of the fortress damaged remain uncertain.

participants: Norse allies named in the annal
warfare.outcome: The fortress was stormed.

entries.title: The Viking Great Army winters at Torksey
entries.dateMeaning: Documented wintering season
entries.summary: A camp’s material record includes coins, metalwork and other evidence of activity beyond the battle narratives.
entries.detail: Agreement between documentary and archaeological evidence clarifies the winter camp’s approximate location and date. A following winter at Repton belongs to a separate phase.
entries.uncertainty: The dates describe one winter. The marker indicates the public locality, not the field boundary or sensitive artifact findspots.

participants: People supplying, trading with or otherwise interacting with the camp
warfare.outcome: The army established a winter base and continued its English campaign afterward.

entries.title: The Viking Great Army winters at Repton
entries.dateMeaning: Documented wintering season
entries.summary: The wintering is cited in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, while archaeological work dates several distinct burials and deposits.
entries.detail: Radiocarbon reassessment examined how marine food consumption affected apparent ages. It supports association of the charnel with the campaign period while leaving individual biographies open.
entries.uncertainty: The map shows the public village and archaeological setting. Assemblages and burial phases need their own chronological treatment.

warfare.outcome: Repton served as a winter base amid a change in Mercian rule.

entries.title: Alfred defeats Guthrum’s army at Ethandun
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Edington and Bratton district, proposed battlefield vicinity
entries.summary: The battle marked a reversal in the struggle over Wessex.
entries.detail: Edington is a strong historical identification for Ethandun. The account of the battle and the later settlement should be kept separate from claims that a particular prehistoric feature was used as part of the encounter.
entries.uncertainty: The point locates the Edington area. The exact battlefield is uncertain.

warfare.outcome: Alfred won the battle and Guthrum subsequently accepted terms.

entries.title: Brega and Leinster forces expel Dublin’s Norse rulers
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The annal records a political and military expulsion from a fortified base.
entries.detail: The episode is distinct from Dublin’s earlier establishment and later reoccupation. Archaeology and political texts address different aspects of whether settlement and activity continued.
entries.uncertainty: The event concerns control of Dublin. It cannot establish the disappearance of all Norse-speaking residents or exchange.

participants: Norse rulers and forces of Dublin
warfare.outcome: The rulers lost their Dublin base; organized Norse power later returned.

entries.title: The men of Fortriu defeat a force led by Ímar’s grandson
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Moray Firth and northern Fortriu context, regional anchor only
entries.summary: An annal attests the continued military activity of a group described as the men of Fortriu in the early tenth century.
entries.detail: The entry is evidence of a distinct confrontation and a named affiliation, nearly two generations after the defeat of Fortriu in 839.
entries.uncertainty: The sources do not locate the encounter exactly. The pin identifies a regional reference area.

participants: Ímar grandson of Ímar and his followers
warfare.outcome: Ímar and many with him were killed.

entries.title: Æthelstan defeats a coalition at Brunanburh
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Wirral district, one proposed battlefield region
entries.summary: Brunanburh brought multiple kings and political interests together in a major tenth-century encounter.
entries.detail: Historical sources attest the battle. Several different locations have been proposed, and the Wirral anchor identifies a candidate area for further inquiry.
entries.uncertainty: The pin is a putative district rather than a confirmed position or footprint.

participants: West Saxon and Mercian forces under Æthelstan and Edmund
Forces associated with Amlaíb of Dublin and King Constantine of Alba and other allies
warfare.outcome: Æthelstan’s forces defeated the opposing coalition.

entries.title: Rivals fight for control of Alba at Dorsum Crup
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Duncrub and Dunning district, Strathearn, proposed locality
entries.summary: The battle offers an example of competition within Alba in the generations after the naming shift from Pictland.
entries.detail: The Scottish Archaeological Research Framework links the site’s probable location to the political relationships among Atholl, Strathearn and royal power.
entries.uncertainty: The place-name identification is probable. The map shows the district and leaves precise positions unassigned.

participants: Forces of King Dub of Alba
Rival coalition including men of Atholl
warfare.outcome: The encounter was won by the king’s side, and the abbot of Dunkeld was among those who fell.

entries.title: Máel Sechnaill defeats Dublin and Isles forces at Tara
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The annal records fighting between a regional Irish king and a coalition connected to Dublin and the Isles.
entries.detail: Accounts of the event have their own rhetoric about foreign power. Norse and Norse-Gaelic activity continued in different settings afterward.
entries.uncertainty: The district is the historical reference. The evidence does not locate each force within the battlefield.

participants: Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill and his forces
Forces from Dublin and the Isles
warfare.outcome: Dublin and Isles forces lost the battle and political pressure on Dublin increased.

entries.title: Viking raiders defeat Byrhtnoth’s force at Maldon
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Maldon and Northey Island crossing area, Essex
entries.summary: The battle near an Essex tidal crossing is documented in chronicle, literary and landscape evidence.
entries.detail: The Old English poem is an important record of the battle’s reception. Its treatment of participants and decisions is a literary interpretation as well as a source.
entries.uncertainty: Exact placements and timing across the tidal landscape are uncertain.

warfare.outcome: Byrhtnoth and many of his men died and the raiders prevailed.

entries.title: Brian Bóruma’s coalition defeats the Leinster–Dublin alliance
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Clontarf brought several political groups from Ireland and the Irish Sea together in opposing alliances.
entries.detail: A victory over a coalition did not end the former port. The museum and annals support a more complex account than a conflict between two homogeneous peoples.
entries.uncertainty: The district marker locates the named battle and leaves precise lines and force sizes uncertain.

participants: Leinster and Dublin forces with allies including from Orkney
warfare.outcome: The Leinster–Dublin coalition was defeated; Brian and other leaders died.

entries.title: Cnut defeats Edmund Ironside’s forces at Assandun
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Ashingdon, Essex, traditional candidate for Assandun
entries.summary: The battle was part of a royal campaign in England financed and conducted across the North Sea.
entries.detail: The agreement after the battle and the sole reign afterward are distinct stages. Cnut’s later association with Denmark and Norway does not make their borders the territory of this battlefield event.
entries.uncertainty: The clash is documentary and the location remains contested. The pin marks the traditional Ashingdon candidate.

warfare.outcome: Cnut’s side prevailed, after which Cnut and Edmund divided authority; Cnut became sole king following Edmund’s death.

entries.title: Óláfr Haraldsson is killed at Stiklestad
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: An attempt to regain power brought an exiled ruler back against opponents with Norwegian support.
entries.detail: Later accounts and the saint’s cult shaped the event’s memory. Their religious interpretation can be examined alongside evidence for political competition over the kingdom.
entries.uncertainty: Stiklestad is an established battlefield locality. Several details are transmitted through later accounts.

participants: Opposing forces drawn from Norwegian regional elites and their supporters
warfare.outcome: Óláfr was killed and his forces were defeated.

entries.title: Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeat the northern earls
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The invasion brought a Norwegian royal army and an English claimant’s allies against regional English forces.
entries.detail: The sources establish the sequence before Stamford Bridge and Hastings. Fulford has more than one proposed battlefield position.
entries.uncertainty: The pin locates the Fulford district and omits any precise formation or route.

participants: Norwegian army of Harald Hardrada and supporters of Tostig
Forces under Earls Edwin and Morcar
warfare.outcome: Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls before the next engagement at Stamford Bridge.

entries.title: Harold Godwinson defeats Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Stamford Bridge on the River Derwent
entries.summary: The English victory ended the Norwegian royal bid of 1066 after Fulford.
entries.detail: The site and event appear in several versions of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The Norwegian army and the English royal force met again as part of a rapidly changing campaign geography.
entries.uncertainty: The approximate marker covers a larger battlefield. Specific positions and detailed later stories remain uncertain.

participants: English royal army under Harold Godwinson
Norwegian army under Harald Hardrada and Tostig’s supporters
warfare.outcome: Harald and Tostig died and the surviving invasion fleet withdrew.

entries.title: Cnut IV’s projected invasion fleet disperses in the Limfjord
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A planned expedition depended on how long crews and magnates would remain mobilized.
entries.detail: The event shows the resource and political limits of royal naval action, including within Denmark. The intended objective never became an actual sailing route.
entries.uncertainty: The marker gives a regional anchor in the Limfjord, whose shape and channels changed. No England route is drawn.

participants: Magnates and crews summoned for the expedition
warfare.outcome: The assembly broke up before an invasion of England took place.

entries.title: Magnus Barelegs’ fleet encounters Norman forces near Anglesey
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Anglesey and the Menai Strait, regional anchor
entries.summary: Norse royal operations intersected with a Norman campaign against Welsh rulers.
entries.detail: Different records emphasize different claims and sides. A Norwegian encounter off Anglesey does not establish long-term sovereignty over the island.
entries.uncertainty: The specific ship and shore positions are debated. The marker gives geographic context for the strait.

participants: Anglo-Norman forces associated with the earls of Shrewsbury and Chester
warfare.outcome: Hugh of Montgomery was killed, and the intervention altered the situation of the forces on Anglesey.

entries.title: Magnus Barelegs dies on a raid in Ulaid
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Eastern Ulster, Down district reference only
entries.summary: The Annals of Ulster name the Norwegian king and place the raid in Ulaid.
entries.detail: The event followed earlier royal expeditions into the Irish Sea and contacts with Irish rulers. Its political context can be traced more confidently than its exact location.
entries.uncertainty: The Irish annal does not give a precise site. The pin is a regional anchor.

participants: Norse expedition led by Magnus Barelegs
warfare.outcome: Magnus was killed and his attempt to extend power ended.

entries.title: Gwenllian’s force confronts the lord of Kidwelly
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A battle in the 1136 uprising linked competing rulers and families in southwest Wales.
entries.detail: Cadw’s account places Gwenllian’s decision within a wider Welsh uprising. Later commemoration and the place of her death have evidence of different kinds.
entries.uncertainty: The pin identifies the Kidwelly locality rather than a surveyed battlefield.

participants: Norman forces under Maurice de Londres
warfare.outcome: Gwenllian’s force was defeated and she was killed.

entries.title: Norse forces capture Rothesay Castle
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A struggle over the western islands left a documented siege at a surviving castle.
entries.detail: Historic Environment Scotland distinguishes this assault from the expedition of 1263, when a force again attacked the same castle.
entries.uncertainty: Interpretation of details rests partly on saga evidence. The castle point has a firmer location than troop movements.

warfare.outcome: The expedition breached and took the castle; its leader died following the action.

entries.title: Norwegian and Scottish forces fight at Largs
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Largs shore district, Firth of Clyde
entries.summary: A storm and fighting on the Scottish shore interrupted Hákon’s western expedition.
entries.detail: The battle belongs in a longer sequence of operations in the Firth of Clyde. The treaty of 1266 is a separate legal milestone.
entries.uncertainty: The point denotes the coastal vicinity, not the position of the later monument or all participants.

participants: Men of King Hákon IV’s Norwegian expedition
Forces of Alexander III of Scotland
warfare.outcome: The fighting did not determine control by itself; Hákon’s expedition withdrew and a later treaty changed sovereignty.

entries.title: Hákon’s expedition again takes Rothesay Castle
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The episode is a second attested capture of the same castle after the siege of 1230.
entries.detail: The return had different participants and political context. The period of capture is distinct from the later legal transfer of the Isles.
entries.uncertainty: The castle is identifiable. The chronology and exact movements of individual forces are less firm.

participants: Norwegian forces associated with Hákon IV’s expedition
warfare.outcome: The Norse retook the castle during the western campaign.

entries.title: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd dies near Cilmeri
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The death of the prince marked a major turn in the conflict over Welsh rule.
entries.detail: Cadw distinguishes the broader campaign and castle building from the event commemorated near Cilmeri.
entries.uncertainty: The monument is at a traditional locality. The precise site of the encounter remains uncertain.

participants: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and Welsh forces
warfare.outcome: Llywelyn was killed during the wider English campaign against his principality.

entries.title: Bruce defeats Comyn’s faction at Barra and Inverurie
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Forces claiming different loyalties within Scotland fought in the aftermath of Bruce’s bid for the crown.
entries.detail: The engagements around Inverurie and Barra belonged to a wider conflict involving the Comyn family, Scottish regional loyalties and English intervention.
entries.uncertainty: Historic Environment Scotland favors 23 May but discusses chronology and conflicting accounts; the marker represents the battlefield area.

warfare.outcome: Bruce defeated a rival political and military faction in northeastern Scotland.

entries.title: Valdemar IV’s army defeats Gotland’s force at Visby
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A battlefield and associated mass graves preserve evidence of people killed outside the city.
entries.detail: Archaeology helps test generalizations about equipment and injury. The city and island communities experienced the campaign in different ways.
entries.uncertainty: The marker stands for the wider battlefield. The location of graves and the area of fighting do not coincide exactly.

warfare.outcome: The Gotlandic force was defeated and the Danes took control of Visby.

entries.title: Owain Glyndŵr’s forces defeat a pursuing army at Bryn Glas
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle was one episode in a wider Welsh revolt with shifting regional loyalties.
entries.detail: The Cadw interpretation plan reviews the evidence for the battlefield and its setting. The revolt continued after the battle with changes in alliances.
entries.uncertainty: The pin indicates the documented landscape near Pilleth. Details of real-time positions and casualty totals remain uncertain.

warfare.outcome: Glyndŵr’s forces prevailed and Mortimer was captured.

entries.title: The Lord of the Isles and the Earl of Mar fight at Harlaw
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The conflict grew from a dispute over Ross and brought forces from both mainland and island districts to Harlaw.
entries.detail: Harlaw’s participants and later representations cannot be reduced to two fixed cultural blocs. Burgh participants sat within one coalition, alongside nobles and regional landholders.
entries.uncertainty: The date and battlefield are documented. Force sizes and claims of outright victory vary across accounts.

participants: Forces of Domhnall, Lord of the Isles
Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar and allied levies
warfare.outcome: Both armies sustained heavy losses; the Lord of the Isles withdrew and the competing claims persisted.

entries.title: Donald Balloch defeats royal forces at Inverlochy
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: River Lochy and Inverlochy Castle vicinity, Lochaber
entries.summary: A campaign to curb the Lordship of the Isles led to a battle beside the River Lochy.
entries.detail: The fighting reveals the reach of different alliances across Lochaber and the Isles, and is a separate event from the battle of 1645 near the same castle.
entries.uncertainty: Sources establish the general location and month. The positions of groups during the encounter are reconstructed.

participants: Donald Balloch and supporters of the Lord of the Isles
warfare.outcome: The forces of Donald Balloch and allies routed the king’s forces.

entries.title: James IV is killed after the Scottish army crosses into Northumberland
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle brought the consequences of war to communities on both sides of the border.
entries.detail: The battlefield register distinguishes the encampment on Flodden Hill from the main engagement near Branxton.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped area identifies the public battlefield district rather than any precise position.

participants: English army under the Earl of Surrey
warfare.outcome: The English forces won and the Scottish king was killed with many nobles and soldiers.

entries.title: Christian II orders executions in the Stockholm Bloodbath
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Stortorget and adjacent old town, Stockholm
entries.summary: The executions followed a political and military struggle over the Swedish throne.
entries.detail: Archaeological, archival and pictorial sources have different purposes. Later accounts connect the event to the end of Christian II’s Swedish rule; imprisonment and seizure of property also mattered.
entries.uncertainty: The map shows old-town context. Details of individual charges and victims vary in records.

participants: Executed Swedish nobles, clerics and burgesses
warfare.outcome: People condemned after Christian II’s coronation were executed; the events helped spur further opposition.

entries.title: English forces defeat the Scottish army at Pinkie
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The encounter was part of pressure for a marriage alliance and control of the young Scottish queen’s future.
entries.detail: The battlefield extends across a coastal and riverine setting outside Edinburgh. Documentary and archaeological evidence can be compared with modern changes to the site.
entries.uncertainty: The map point represents a larger battlefield, and reported losses vary by source.

participants: English army under the Duke of Somerset
Scottish army under the Earl of Arran
warfare.outcome: The English army defeated the force defending Scotland during the Rough Wooing.

entries.title: Mary’s supporters lose to Regent Moray’s forces at Langside
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Scottish factions confronted each other over rule following Mary’s escape from Loch Leven.
entries.detail: The localized battle arose from a larger contest over royal authority, regency and succession. The modern city covers the battlefield landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The historical event is dated. The map marker identifies the wider locality rather than a particular formation.

participants: Mary, Queen of Scots and her supporters
warfare.outcome: Moray’s forces prevailed and Mary fled, subsequently crossing into England.

entries.title: Catholic earls defeat an army at Glenlivet
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Competing noble factions fought in a conflict tied to religion, political power and royal authority.
entries.detail: The encounter reveals that post-Reformation Scottish allegiances could cross regional and kinship lines. In the aftermath the monarchy still had to negotiate with powerful noble groups.
entries.uncertainty: The battlefield inventory assesses later accounts and the wider landscape. Recorded manpower and casualties are uncertain.

participants: Earls of Huntly and Errol and their forces
Earl of Argyll and royal forces
warfare.outcome: The forces of Huntly and Errol defeated the army commanded by Argyll.

entries.title: Cudgel War forces fight around Nokia manor
entries.dateMeaning: Turn-of-year window reported by the City of Nokia
entries.place: Nokia manor district, Pirkkala historical setting
entries.summary: The city’s historical account identifies the local fighting as decisive for this phase of the Cudgel War.
entries.detail: A movement rooted in peasant grievances expanded across regions and met opposition from armed authorities. The Nokia phase was only one part of the conflict.
entries.uncertainty: This date window crosses the turn of the year. The pin marks the documented district and does not locate a particular day of fighting.

participants: Forces defending the Swedish realm’s local military administration
warfare.outcome: The rebel force at Nokia was defeated during the wider uprising.

entries.title: Montrose defeats Covenanter forces outside Perth
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: A royalist army with forces brought by Alasdair Mac Colla fought a Covenanter force near Perth.
entries.detail: This episode places the Scottish Civil War within connected conflicts in Britain and Ireland. Forces mobilized under different legal, religious and political loyalties.
entries.uncertainty: The marker indicates the battlefield district. The identity and size of individual units vary in accounts.

participants: Royalists under Montrose with Alasdair Mac Colla
warfare.outcome: Royalist victory enabled entry into Perth and opened Montrose’s Scottish campaign.

entries.title: Royalists defeat Baillie’s Covenanters at Alford
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Combatants from opposing political coalitions confronted each other near Alford in the summer campaign.
entries.detail: The HES inventory sets the engagement among other movements and encounters of the civil war. The landscape records field conditions that have been interpreted differently by historians.
entries.uncertainty: The battle has a known regional setting. Physical finds securely attributable to it remain sparse.

warfare.outcome: Montrose’s forces defeated the Covenanter army and continued toward the Lowlands.

entries.title: Montrose defeats Sir John Hurry at Auldearn
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Fighting near Auldearn again pitted Scottish Royalists and Covenanters against each other.
entries.detail: The historic battlefield assessment compares different accounts of where people fought. Associating a named commander with a side in this battle does not describe permanent allegiances across the wider conflict.
entries.uncertainty: The placement of several phases of fighting remains debated. The map shows the village-area battlefield anchor.

participants: Royalists under Montrose and Alasdair Mac Colla
warfare.outcome: Royalists defeated a Covenanter army during Montrose’s campaign.

entries.title: Montrose and Mac Colla defeat Covenanters at Inverlochy
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Inverlochy Castle and River Lochy vicinity
entries.summary: Forces within Scotland, including men with Irish connections, fought near the castle in a phase of civil war.
entries.detail: The Royalist campaign intersected with local loyalties and had a lasting record in verse and music as well as written accounts. The 1431 conflict near the same castle belongs to a different period.
entries.uncertainty: The approximate marker is shared with the wider battlefield landscape. The sources disagree about details of troop deployments.

participants: Royalists under Montrose and Alasdair Mac Colla
Covenanter forces under the Earl of Argyll and Duncan Campbell of Auchinbreck
warfare.outcome: Royalist forces won a major victory over Argyll’s Covenanters.

entries.title: Royalists defeat Covenanters at Kilsyth
entries.dateMeaning: Event date in the inventory header and a contemporary account
entries.summary: The battle was a major Royalist victory during a short period of shifting control.
entries.detail: The HES inventory describes an area covering several possible alignments and considers changes to the land, including the later loch. Its event header and a contemporary account give 15 August.
entries.uncertainty: The inventory also gives 16 August in a later summary. The date shown uses the header and contemporary account, and the pin identifies the district.

participants: Royalists under Montrose and Alasdair Mac Colla
warfare.outcome: Montrose’s Royalists defeated Baillie’s Covenanter army.

entries.title: Covenanter forces defeat Montrose at Philiphaugh
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The defeat near Selkirk reversed gains Royalists had made in the preceding battles.
entries.detail: The battlefield history includes the fate of surrendering troops and people traveling with the army. Different accounts require separate readings of the battle and its aftermath.
entries.uncertainty: The pin is a battlefield anchor and does not identify where particular deaths or captures took place.

warfare.outcome: Leslie defeated Montrose’s army, ending this phase of the Royalist campaign.

entries.title: Battle of Carbisdale
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: Carbisdale, near the Kyle of Sutherland
entries.summary: A new Royalist campaign ended in a clash in northern Scotland.
entries.detail: The battle reflected changed alliances after the execution of Charles I and the renewed effort by Montrose to rally supporters for Charles II.
entries.uncertainty: The anchor locates the conflict area near the river. Montrose’s capture took place at a different location.

participants: Covenanters and northern levies under forces of the Scottish government
warfare.outcome: Montrose’s army was defeated; he was captured later.

entries.title: Battle of Dunbar II
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The opposing armies fought outside Dunbar during the third civil war phase.
entries.detail: The battle followed the Scottish proclamation of Charles II and an English invasion. Its aftermath included the forced march and detention of prisoners.
entries.uncertainty: The point is a battlefield district anchor. Prisoners reached several later destinations.

participants: English Parliamentarian army under Oliver Cromwell
warfare.outcome: Cromwell’s army won a major victory, and many Scottish soldiers were taken prisoner.

entries.title: Copenhagen’s defenders repel a Swedish assault
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle came as Swedish forces renewed their campaign after the Treaty of Roskilde.
entries.detail: The date pertains to the main assault during a longer siege. Accounts describe multiple parts of the city defenses and record different participants’ roles.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks a surviving central anchor. It does not describe the extent of the siege works.

participants: Swedish forces under Charles X Gustav
Copenhagen defenders and the Danish crown
warfare.outcome: The assault failed and the city held.

entries.title: Swedish forces defeat the Danish army near Lund
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.place: North of Lund, Scanian War battlefield district
entries.summary: Two crowns fought for control in Skåne after earlier territorial transfers.
entries.detail: The battle was one phase of the Scanian War. That war’s eventual settlement and the effects on local populations require evidence beyond the battle outcome.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks the broader battlefield district. Reported figures for losses depend on source and scope.

warfare.outcome: The Swedish army won a costly victory.

entries.title: Battle of Bothwell Bridge
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The two sides fought around the Clyde crossing during the 1679 rebellion.
entries.detail: The bridge physically connects the locality to the surviving evidence, although fighting extended beyond the bridge itself. The defeat brought extensive arrests and imprisonment.
entries.uncertainty: The inventory gives 22 June and records a wider battlefield around the bridge. The pin is its general inventory reference point.

participants: Government forces under the Duke of Monmouth
warfare.outcome: Government troops captured the crossing, defeated the Covenanter army and took prisoners.

entries.title: Battle of Drumclog
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: An attempt to suppress a field religious gathering led to fighting.
entries.detail: The encounter opened a short sequence that ended weeks later with Covenanter defeat at Bothwell Bridge. Both episodes were fought amid religious regulation and local mobilization.
entries.uncertainty: The marker locates the recorded area rather than all positions described in retrospective accounts.

participants: Government troops under John Graham of Claverhouse
warfare.outcome: The Covenanters repelled the first government force sent against them.

entries.title: Battle of Dunkeld
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The fighting spread through Dunkeld itself less than a month after Killiecrankie.
entries.detail: The engagement documents another set of Scottish loyalties. The town and cathedral surroundings form part of the recorded account and show why its civilian setting matters.
entries.uncertainty: The map identifies the town near the center of the encounter, with several distinct positions described in the source.

warfare.outcome: The defenders held the town and the Jacobites withdrew.

entries.title: Battle of Killiecrankie
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The conflict brought opposing Scottish forces and other supporters into the first Jacobite rising.
entries.detail: The battlefield lies in a narrow Highland landscape. The government’s next confrontation at Dunkeld unfolded after the Jacobites lost their commander.
entries.uncertainty: The exact placement of units and estimates of casualties vary.

participants: Jacobites under John Graham of Claverhouse
warfare.outcome: The Jacobites won, but their commander was killed.

entries.title: Battle of Cromdale
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Pressure on surviving Jacobite forces led to a battle in the Cromdale district.
entries.detail: Historic Environment Scotland distinguishes military and later commemorative accounts. This was an episode in the wider first Jacobite rising in Scotland.
entries.uncertainty: The historically described movements cover a broader area than shown by the anchor.

participants: Government forces under Sir Thomas Livingstone
warfare.outcome: Government forces broke up the Jacobite force.

entries.title: Russian forces defeat Armfelt at Napue
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle brought locally recruited defenders and wider armies into the Great Northern War in Ostrobothnia.
entries.detail: The heritage register documents the vicinity and place of commemoration. The prolonged civilian consequences of Russian occupation are a separate history.
entries.uncertainty: The marker identifies the battlefield district; figures for combatants and losses are estimates.

participants: Swedish realm forces under Carl Gustaf Armfelt and local recruits
warfare.outcome: The Russian army defeated Armfelt’s forces.

entries.title: Battle of Sheriffmuir
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The two sides contested a position above Dunblane in the main Scottish engagement of the 1715 rising.
entries.detail: The outcome is more intelligible at campaign scale than as a single winner on the field. Fighting and deployments extended across a wider upland area.
entries.uncertainty: Descriptions of a decisive tactical victory overstate the evidence.

participants: Jacobites under the Earl of Mar
Government forces under the Duke of Argyll
warfare.outcome: Each army claimed success, while the rising lost momentum and failed to secure its objectives.

entries.title: Akershus is attacked during the Swedish campaign
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Akershus became the focus of attack during a Great Northern War incursion into Norway.
entries.detail: The city and fortress had distinct experiences of the campaign, which forms a different episode from the later Swedish siege at Fredriksten.
entries.uncertainty: The fortress is an established reference point. The map does not reconstruct approaches or defensive positions.

warfare.outcome: The fortress withstood the Swedish campaign.

entries.title: Charles XII dies during the siege of Fredriksten
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The attack on the southeastern frontier formed part of a new Swedish campaign in Norway.
entries.detail: The fortress was attacked at several times. It provides a fixed point for a conflict whose political reach was much wider than the battlefield.
entries.uncertainty: The reason and direction of the fatal shot remain disputed. The marker locates the fortress complex.

warfare.outcome: Charles XII was killed and Swedish forces abandoned the siege.

entries.title: Battle of Glenshiel
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The brief 1719 rising included a Spanish intervention and a Highland battlefield.
entries.detail: Surviving remains give evidence for the location and setting of aspects of the fighting. The Jacobite cause linked Scottish supporters to a wider European conflict.
entries.uncertainty: The pin indicates the battlefield district and does not describe precise movements.

warfare.outcome: Government troops defeated the Jacobite and Spanish force.

entries.title: Battle of Prestonpans
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle near the coast changed control and confidence in the early campaign.
entries.detail: Government reports and other accounts preserve dates, though the changes to the local landscape and archaeological survey add separate evidence.
entries.uncertainty: The marker is a locality anchor for a landscape spanning multiple positions.

participants: Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart
warfare.outcome: Jacobite forces defeated the government army early in the rising.

entries.title: Battle of Falkirk II
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The largest Jacobite army of the 1745 rising met government troops near Falkirk.
entries.detail: The victory formed part of a longer campaign whose course changed soon afterward. Original plans and reports use differing conventions and cover distinct perspectives.
entries.uncertainty: The location marks a wider battlefield. An eighteenth-century drawing cited by the inventory gives a different day in its caption.

participants: Jacobite forces under Charles Edward Stuart
warfare.outcome: The Jacobites defeated Hawley’s government army but did not secure a lasting strategic advantage.

entries.title: The Swedish fleet defeats the Russian fleet at Svensksund
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Wrecks and archival records document the naval conflict in channels outside present-day Kotka.
entries.detail: Maritime archaeology identifies some individual vessels and contexts, and continues to distinguish wrecks from different activities and engagements near the same waters.
entries.uncertainty: The map gives a broad waterway anchor rather than battle lines or wreck positions.

warfare.outcome: The Swedish fleet won the second battle in the area.

entries.title: British and Danish fleets fight off Copenhagen
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The naval battle was fought near Copenhagen during a dispute over wartime neutrality and trade.
entries.detail: Maritime archaeological work on Dannebroge and contemporary records provide distinct strands of evidence. This was an earlier event than the bombardment of the city in 1807.
entries.uncertainty: The point locates the offshore district. Individual positions and wrecks require separately mapped sources.

warfare.outcome: The British attack forced a ceasefire and negotiations after heavy losses.

entries.title: Copenhagen capitulates after British bombardment
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The bombardment damaged the city and affected its civilians as well as the defending forces.
entries.detail: The capitulation text dated 7 September specifies terms after the bombardment. It supplies stronger evidence for surrender terms than for every event within the city.
entries.uncertainty: The pin shows the city involved. It does not mark any firing site, house or legal boundary.

warfare.outcome: Danish authorities capitulated and surrendered the fleet under the written agreement.

entries.title: Russian forces defeat the Swedish army at Oravais
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The battle turned the late summer campaign in Ostrobothnia.
entries.detail: The local battlefield institution gives a chronology based on accounts of the fighting. It also documents the district and ways the event has been remembered locally.
entries.uncertainty: The position is an anchor for a series of engagements rather than a formation or troop line.

warfare.outcome: The Russian side prevailed and the Swedish forces withdrew.

entries.title: Russian forces take Viapori / Sveaborg after siege
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The capture was a major episode in the 1808–09 war.
entries.detail: The islands formed a military and civilian community. The fortress’s later administration differed from that of the autonomous Grand Duchy around it.
entries.uncertainty: The pin identifies the fortress group. The legal transfer of Finland followed at a separate date.

warfare.outcome: The garrison surrendered in May and the fortress passed to Russia.

entries.title: Danish forces break the siege of Fredericia
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The engagement around the fortress town became a major event in the First Schleswig War.
entries.detail: The locality records both military construction and subsequent commemoration. The broader war’s political and territorial outcomes took longer to resolve.
entries.uncertainty: The anchor marks the fortress town and the engagement extended beyond the walls.

warfare.outcome: The Danish attack forced the besieging army to withdraw.

entries.title: French and British forces take Bomarsund
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: Åland became a theater of the Crimean War through its Russian fortress.
entries.detail: The present ruins show parts of the undertaking and the destructive aftermath. The later legal demilitarization of Åland was a separate development.
entries.uncertainty: The main fortress anchor does not include all outworks or attack sites.

warfare.outcome: The Russian fortress capitulated and was subsequently demolished.

entries.title: French and British ships bombard Viapori
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the recorded conflict event
entries.summary: The fortress was attacked during the Crimean War after a separate siege in 1808 had transferred it to Russia.
entries.detail: The archive and remaining structures contain evidence of damage and later repair. The military chronology and the history of residents in the islands require different records.
entries.uncertainty: The pin locates the island complex and leaves ships’ positions and firing lines unassigned.

participants: Russian garrison and defenders of Viapori
warfare.outcome: The bombardment inflicted significant damage but did not capture the fortress.
